subject: Business
title: Choice Overload: When More Is Less
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Choice Overload: When More Is Less.

hook.text: A supermarket offered 24 jams for tasting. Only 3% bought. With 6 jams, 30% bought. Fewer options, more sales.

buildup.text: Sheena Iyengar's jam study proved that too many options paralyze decision-making.

discovery.text: When choices overwhelm us, we defer the decision — which often means buying nothing at all.

twist.text: Yet consumers say they want more options. They prefer the idea of choice more than the reality of choosing.

climax.text: Apple offers a few products. Amazon offers millions but curates with 'Best Sellers' and 'Amazon's Choice.'

punchline.text: Don't offer everything. Curate the best few.

quiz.question: What did the jam study demonstrate?
options: Too many options paralyze decisions and reduce purchases
Expensive jams sell better than cheap ones

details.summary: Choice overload occurs when too many options paralyze decision-making, leading to anxiety, decision avoidance, or dissatisfaction with the chosen option. Sheena Iyengar's famous jam study showed that offering 24 varieties reduced purchases by 90 percent compared to offering only 6 flavors.
details.whyItMatters: Businesses assume more choices attract more customers. In reality, excessive choice creates cognitive burden that drives people away.
takeaways: Too many choices paralyze decisions and reduce overall purchase rates
Iyengar's jam study showed 24 options generated 90 percent fewer purchases than 6
Curating options and simplifying choices increases conversion and satisfaction

faq.question: How many options should businesses offer to maximize sales?
faq.answer: Research suggests three to five options often optimize the balance between variety and simplicity. Categorizing choices into clear groups helps when more variety is necessary. Providing a recommended or most popular option reduces cognitive burden even within larger sets.

faq.question: Why does having too many choices lead to dissatisfaction with the chosen option?
faq.answer: With many alternatives, people imagine the unchosen options might have been better. This counterfactual thinking creates regret. With fewer options, the comparison set is smaller and easier to evaluate. Less choice means less opportunity for second-guessing the purchase after the fact.
